case_studies.title: Sacred Metrics
case_studies.one_liner: Closing the conversion gap for a 20-year wellness brand
meta: GA4, Ahrefs, Crazy Egg, Lighthouse, ChatGPT (AI visibility testing), Figma, WordPress
case_studies.summary: A 20-year-old wellness brand in Ubud, Bali with strong organic traffic, genuine guest loyalty, and a domain rating of 62 backed by 13.5K backlinks. The brief: modernise the digital experience, close the gap between offline reputation and online conversion, and assess AI search readiness.
sections: The opportunity

Guest sentiment was overwhelmingly positive, "lush green oasis," "feels less like a studio and more like a community," but the website led with schedules and logistics rather than the atmosphere that actually drives bookings. The brand had significant digital equity that wasn't being fully leveraged: strong organic positions, loyal repeat visitors, and a product guests already loved. The question was how to make the website work as hard as the experience itself.
The approach

Six detailed UX/CRO flow walkthroughs (Homepage, Schedule, Workshops/Ecstatic Dance, Retreats, Accommodation, Wellness) with heuristic scoring and annotated wireframes. Crazy Egg session recordings and heatmaps to validate UX/CRO findings with observed user behaviour. Full technical audit covering Core Web Vitals, platform security, and migration risk analysis for a schedule page carrying a significant share of all organic sessions. SEO health assessment and Google Business Profile competitive benchmarking. AI search visibility testing across five ChatGPT queries, confirming top-3 positioning. AISO/GEO foundational layer assessment. End-to-end measurement architecture review across both booking systems and GA4.
What shipped

An 81-page audit document with approximately 90 PIE-scored findings, a phased action roadmap across four phases and seven workstreams, and annotated Figma wireframes for all six flows. The roadmap sequenced work across technical foundations, measurement, CTA alignment, redirect mapping, and design refresh, each phase unlocking the next. Visual direction recommendations preserved Balinese cultural identity while moving toward a lighter, nature-grounded wellness aesthetic.
The impact

The audit gave the team an evidence-based foundation for prioritising work across UX, CRO, SEO, design, and technical infrastructure simultaneously, replacing ad hoc fixes with a sequenced strategy tied to measurable outcomes. Because the roadmap was phased and each recommendation came with concrete implementation steps, the team could act on findings immediately rather than scoping the work first.

case_studies.title: The Collective
case_studies.highlight: Turning a high-authority wellness directory into the year-round heartbeat of a three-property ecosystem
meta: Strategic Direction, Conversion, UX, SEO & AI Visibility
GA4, Ahrefs, Crazy Egg, Lighthouse, ChatGPT (AI visibility testing), Google Rich Results, Figma, WordPress
case_studies.summary: A decade-old wellness directory in Bali with 885 referring domains, Wikipedia citations on its cultural content, and a position in 165 Google AI Overviews — operating within a three-property ecosystem that included a physical yoga studio and an annual wellness festival under the same ownership. The site had significant domain authority and editorial assets, but no defined strategic role within the ecosystem. The brief: assess the site's current state, define a strategic direction for the platform, and deliver a conversion-ready roadmap that connects it to the broader ecosystem.
sections: The opportunity

The site's editorial content was quietly outperforming its directory function — three of the top five pages by traffic were blog articles, not listings. A single ceremony page had earned backlinks from three Wikipedia articles. The retreat and accommodation directories showed the longest session durations on the site (above one minute), confirming visitor intent to compare and decide. This was a platform with proven editorial authority and engaged audiences, ready for a strategic model that could channel that attention into something more purposeful. The competitor landscape revealed white space: established publishers owned the content lane, booking platforms owned the transaction lane, but no one held the community position — connecting practitioners, travellers, and locals year-round.
The approach

Stakeholder interview covering site history, team capabilities, competitor positioning, CMS constraints, and ecosystem dynamics. Strategic direction analysis evaluating four alternatives (tourist guide, cultural storytelling, curated marketplace, community platform) against current assets and available resources. UX/CRO walkthroughs of the five highest-traffic pages with heuristic scoring, annotated wireframes, and Crazy Egg behavioural validation. Full technical audit including Core Web Vitals, site health scoring, and CMS migration assessment. Backlink profile analysis and anchor text quality review. SEO keyword analysis confirming cultural content as the site's ranking strength over commercial terms. AI visibility testing across four commercial queries, mapping the gap between the site's existing AI citations (cultural content) and the queries the new strategic direction would need to own. Rebrand and visual direction with a shared colour system across the three-property ecosystem.
What shipped

A 50-page audit document with approximately 40 PIE-scored findings, a phased roadmap across five phases (direction decision, foundation launch, community growth, monetisation, ecosystem maturity), and annotated Figma wireframes for all five flows. The centrepiece was a strategic direction recommendation: reposition the site as a curated community platform anchored by a WhatsApp Community, a newsletter, and a member directory — with a website application form gating entry and ecosystem integration giving members tangible benefits across all three properties. The roadmap included a CMS migration plan with plugin stack, a tiered redirect strategy protecting the site's highest-value URLs, a community onboarding flow, and a monetisation model built on promoted listings and paid membership tiers. Visual direction established a shared terracotta colour system across the ecosystem, with distinct accent colours differentiating each property. The naming recommendation gave the community a verbal identity designed for belonging rather than consumption.
The impact

The audit reframed the internal conversation from "what do we do with this site" to "this site is the connective tissue of the ecosystem." The strategic direction gave the client a decision framework — three specific Phase 0 decisions — rather than an open-ended list of improvements. The redesign and visual unification unlocked the highest-value SEO opportunity available: ecosystem cross-linking between two high-authority domains that no amount of external link building could replicate. The project manager's immediate response to the community model: "Love the community ideas" — followed by tactical questions about implementation, confirming the direction landed as actionable rather than aspirational.

case_studies.title: Prima Materia
meta: Everything — positioning, copy, UX, design, development
Custom code, Claude Code, GitHub Pages
HTML/CSS/JS, Claude Code, Figma, GitHub Pages
case_studies.summary: Applying conversion thinking to my own coaching practice.
sections: The context

I'm a somatic coach working with the five elements and alchemical frameworks. Most practitioners in this space build websites that speak to peers — dense with modality language, light on structure, and unclear on what a visitor should actually do. I wanted to build mine the way I'd build a client's: conversion-first, with every section earning its place in the funnel.
The decisions

The page follows a single narrative arc: recognition → education → credibility → action. It opens with "You're here because" — mirroring the visitor's internal state before explaining anything. By the time the Five Elements framework appears, the visitor is already seeing themselves in the work. The about section deliberately leads with my engineering and neuroscience background before somatic training, because the people I want to work with tend to be analytical thinkers who need permission to trust the body. That sequencing is intentional.

"Book a Discovery Call" appears four times. Each placement follows a natural decision point rather than interrupting the reading flow — after the emotional hook, after the framework, after the credibility section, and at the close. One CTA, one action, no ambiguity.
The build

Custom-coded rather than built on a page builder — partly because I wanted full control over performance and structure, and partly because building it with Claude Code was a chance to work the way I advise clients to think: start with the conversion logic, then design to serve it. Hosted on GitHub Pages for speed and simplicity. The visual direction uses black-and-white photography, alchemical symbols, and generous whitespace to signal calm seriousness without the pastel-and-script aesthetic that dominates the wellness space.
Why this matters in my portfolio

The other case studies in this portfolio show how I think about other people's digital experiences. This one shows I hold myself to the same standard — clear positioning, a defined audience, a structured funnel, and design choices that serve conversion rather than decoration.

case_studies.title: NeuroBoost UX
case_studies.one_liner: Uncovering what drives user decisions when surveys and click data can't
case_studies.summary: Two unrelated projects, the same blind spot: teams making product and marketing decisions based on what users said they wanted, while the numbers kept disagreeing. A digital product team's adoption metrics didn't match glowing survey feedback. An automotive brand couldn't settle on a newsletter layout from stakeholder opinion alone. The brief in both cases: measure what users can't self-report.
sections: The problem
Two projects, same blind spot. In both cases, teams were making product and marketing decisions based on what users said they wanted, and the numbers kept disagreeing.

Project 1: a digital product team struggling with engagement. Users completed surveys, gave feedback, clicked through prototypes. Everything looked fine on paper. But adoption metrics told a different story. The team suspected the disconnect was somewhere between what users consciously reported and what actually drove their behaviour, but they had no way to see it.
Project 2: an automotive brand preparing a newsletter relaunch. Three layout variants looked equally strong in internal review. Stakeholders had opinions. Nobody had evidence.
What I did
Online neuromarketing studies (Project 1)

I designed and ran online studies that bypassed self-reported preference entirely. Instead of asking users what they wanted, I measured what was happening underneath: implicit attention patterns, reaction-time-based association tasks, and structured decision games that surface subconscious drivers (the needs and motivations users act on but can't articulate in a survey).

The raw output wasn't a single "winner." It was clusters. Users grouped into distinct segments based on which subconscious needs were actually steering their decisions: security, novelty, status, autonomy, belonging. Each cluster responded to different triggers, different framings, different value propositions.

From those clusters, a set of concrete adaptation recommendations was developed: how to adjust the product's messaging, onboarding flow, and feature hierarchy to speak to each group's actual motivators rather than their stated ones.
A/B/C eye-tracking study (Project 2)

For the automotive client, I built three newsletter variants in HTML/CSS and ran a controlled eye-tracking study across all three. Each participant worked through a realistic reading scenario while gaze data captured fixation duration, scan paths, and which content blocks actually held attention versus which ones users scrolled past.

The study didn't just pick a winner. It showed why one variant outperformed. Heatmaps revealed that the best-converting layout wasn't the one with the strongest hero image or the boldest CTA. It was the one where the visual hierarchy guided the eye through a specific content sequence: context first, then proof, then action. The other two variants scattered attention across competing elements and lost readers before they reached the conversion point.
What shipped

Project 1: A segmentation framework mapping user clusters to their subconscious need profiles, paired with prioritised design and copy recommendations for each segment. The product team stopped guessing which value proposition to lead with and started matching messaging to the actual drivers behind user decisions.

Project 2: A clear recommendation backed by physiological data, not stakeholder preference. The winning newsletter variant, annotated with gaze-pattern analysis showing exactly which layout decisions created the attention flow that drove conversion. The two losing variants got the same treatment: specific, visual evidence of where and why they failed.
The takeaway

Standard testing captures what people are willing and able to tell you. Neuromarketing methods capture what they can't. In both projects, the gap between those two was exactly where the problem lived, and exactly where the solution came from.

case_studies.title: Conversion Engine
case_studies.one_liner: Optimising checkout, product pages, and launch strategy from inside the team
meta: Checkout, Cart, Homepage PDP & Product Launches
Hotjar, GA4, Shopify, A/B testing (Google Optimize), Figma
case_studies.summary: A direct-to-consumer brand with healthy traffic but underperforming conversion. As shop manager and developer, I owned the full e-commerce operation — from product launches and shop optimisation to A/B testing and checkout improvements.
sections: The opportunity

A direct-to-consumer brand with a solid e-commerce operation: healthy traffic, steady sales, a product that resonated. Nothing was broken. But the team knew there was room to convert more of the traffic they were already paying for. The shop had grown organically without a structured optimisation process, which meant small friction points in the cart, checkout, product pages, and mobile experience had accumulated without anyone measuring their actual impact.
The approach

As shop manager and developer, I owned the full e-commerce operation, not just the analysis. I combined session recordings and heatmaps with a full funnel teardown, from ad landing to order confirmation, to pinpoint where the real conversion gaps were versus where the team assumed they might be.

Instead of auditing from outside and handing over a report, I prioritised findings by expected lift versus effort and shipped the fixes myself: checkout form improvements, shipping-cost transparency, mobile PDP layout adjustments. For higher-risk changes, I set up A/B tests to validate before full rollout. New product launches ran in parallel, each one informed by what the data was showing about user behaviour on existing pages.
What shipped

A systematic programme of improvements across homepage, cart, checkout, product detail pages, team page, and mobile experience, prioritised, tested, and deployed. Three A/B tests validated the highest-risk changes before committing. Product launches were integrated into the optimisation cycle rather than treated as separate events.
The impact

Cart abandonment and mobile bounce both improved within the first month of the priority fixes going live. More importantly, the shop moved from ad-hoc fixes to a repeatable optimisation process: structured measurement, prioritised backlog, test before you commit. That process kept producing gains well beyond the initial round of changes.

case_studies.title: Resonance Tunes
meta: Information Architecture, UX/UI Design & Webflow Development
case_studies.summary: Designing and building the business website for an ethical-AI wellness platform from scratch.
sections: The context

Resonance Tunes is an ethical-AI and consciousness technology startup combining somatic science, archetypal psychology, and regenerative systems design. The platform targets two distinct audiences — individuals seeking nervous system regulation and organisations pursuing DEI-integrated wellness — each with different entry points and different levels of familiarity with the concepts. As Product & Technology Innovation Lead within a C-level team, I owned the information architecture, UX/UI design, and full Webflow build. Copy and brand messaging were provided by the founding team.
The design challenge

Consciousness technology is a hard sell visually. Lean too far into tech aesthetics and you lose the somatic, human-centred audience. Lean too far into wellness and you lose credibility with organisational buyers and investors. The site needed to hold both — grounding complex ideas in clean visual hierarchy while signalling that this is a serious platform, not a mood board.

The information architecture had to serve three jobs simultaneously: explain what Resonance Tunes is (brand storytelling), show what it does (product clarity for individuals and groups), and establish legitimacy (testimonials, team, and market positioning) — all without overwhelming a first-time visitor who may have no reference point for "ethical-AI consciousness technology."
The approach

I started with the messaging hierarchy: what does someone need to understand in what order? The homepage opens with the mission, moves to the three market problems the platform addresses (each grounded with a specific statistic), then breaks into audience-specific value propositions before social proof and a blog section. The structure is intentionally conventional — familiar patterns doing the heavy lifting so the unfamiliar content can breathe.

The visual direction balances nature imagery with geometric elements and a calming colour palette that reads as both tech-forward and human-centred. Typography and spacing do most of the work: generous whitespace gives dense concepts room, and clear section breaks prevent the cognitive overload that concept-heavy sites tend to create.

The dual-audience problem was solved with distinct content blocks — "For Individuals" and "For Groups" — each with their own language register and CTAs, so neither audience has to wade through content meant for the other.
The build

The site was built entirely in Webflow, with responsive layouts, CMS-driven blog content, and interaction design that reinforces the brand's emphasis on coherence and flow. The build prioritised clean, maintainable structure over visual complexity — important for an early-stage venture where the site will evolve as the product matures.
Scope of ownership

This was a zero-to-one build within a founding team. Working alongside the CEO and C-level leadership, I translated the company's vision into a structured digital experience: information architecture, visual design system, page design across all sections, and a production Webflow build — giving a pre-revenue startup the credibility to open conversations with practitioners, organisations, and investors.

about.heading: Hi, I'm Imen.
paragraphs: I'm a UX, CRO, and digital strategy consultant based in Berlin. I work with e-commerce, wellness, and SaaS brands that know their product is strong but suspect their website is leaving money on the table. My job is to find out where and fix it — through conversion audits, UX redesigns, landing page builds, and structured A/B testing.

I've spent 10+ years moving between corporate innovation and independent work. At Deloitte, Siemens, and BMW I learned how large organisations approach product, research, and scale. On my own, I learned how to ship fast, prioritise ruthlessly, and make every recommendation something a small team can actually implement. I bring both.

My background is technical — IT and Electrical Engineering at TU Munich — and I worked in neuromarketing at the Deloitte Neuroscience Institute, which means I don't just look at heatmaps and analytics. I understand how attention, trust, and decision-making work at a cognitive level, and I design for that.
Fluent in German, English, French, and Arabic. Based in Berlin, working internationally.

items.q: How does a typical project start?
items.a: Every project begins with a free discovery call. I'll review your homepage or shop on the spot, give you three actionable tips, and we'll figure out together whether there's a fit. If there is, you'll get a clear proposal with scope, timeline, and pricing within a few days.

items.q: How long does a project take?
items.a: A UX/CRO audit typically takes 2–4 weeks. A landing page redesign can be live within a week. Full website and shop builds run 4–8 weeks depending on scope. I'll give you a realistic timeline in the proposal — and flag it early if anything shifts.

items.q: What platforms do you work with?
items.a: Webflow, Shopify, Framer, WordPress, and Squarespace. I'll recommend the platform that fits your team's technical comfort and long-term needs — not the one I prefer.

It depends on scope. Audits start from a fixed price; design and build projects are scoped individually. You'll always get a clear quote before we start. Payment is split into three milestones: 30% upfront, 40% at interim review, 30% on delivery.
Yes. I'm based in Berlin and work with clients internationally. Communication runs through email, video calls, and shared Figma files. Timezone overlaps have never been a problem.

items.q: Who do you work best with?
items.a: E-commerce, wellness, and SaaS brands that already have traffic or a product — but suspect their website isn't converting the way it should. If you're past the "just need a website" stage and into "need the website to perform," we'll get along.

I hand over everything your team needs to maintain the site independently — documentation, logins, and a walkthrough if needed. If you want ongoing optimisation or A/B testing support, we can set that up too.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.content_html:
Last updated: August 28, 2026

This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, and protect your personal data in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and applicable German data protection laws.

1. Controller

Imen Bouzouita
Mahlower Strasse 14
12049 Berlin
Germany

2. Data We Collect

This site collects only what's needed to respond to enquiries and to operate securely. Depending on how you interact with the site, this may include:

  • Identification data (e.g., name)
  • Contact data (e.g., email address)
  • Usage data (e.g., pages visited, interaction data)
  • Technical data (e.g., IP address, browser type, device information), logged by hosting infrastructure

Specifically: contact form submissions (name, email, message) submitted via the contact form, processed through Formspree; Calendly booking details, handled under Calendly's own privacy policy; technical and connection data (e.g. IP address) processed by Cloudflare, our content delivery, DNS, and security provider, for every visitor as part of operating this site; messages sent to our @imenbouzouita.com address, forwarded via Cloudflare Email Routing; and, only if you accept the cookie banner, anonymised usage data collected via Google Analytics (GA4).

3. Legal Basis for Processing

We process your personal data based on the following legal grounds:

  • Consent (Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR)
  • Contract performance (Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR)
  • Legal obligation (Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR)
  • Legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR)

4. Purpose of Data Processing

Your data is processed for the following purposes:

  • Providing and maintaining our services
  • Responding to enquiries and managing booked calls
  • Improving user experience
  • Ensuring security and preventing fraud

5. Data Sharing

We do not sell your personal data. It isn't shared with third parties beyond what's required to operate this site, and only:

  • When required by law
  • With service providers under data processing agreements — currently Formspree (contact form processing), Calendly (call booking), Cloudflare (content delivery, DNS, security, email forwarding, and cookieless web analytics), and, only with your consent, Google Analytics (GA4, usage analytics)
  • With your explicit consent

6. International Data Transfers

Some of our service providers, including Formspree, Calendly, Cloudflare, and Google (Google Analytics), are based outside the European Economic Area (EEA). Where data is transferred outside the EEA, we ensure appropriate safeguards such as Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs).

7. Data Retention

We retain personal data only as long as necessary for the purposes stated above or as required by law.

8. Your Rights

Under GDPR, you have the following rights:

  • Right of access (Art. 15 GDPR)
  • Right to rectification (Art. 16 GDPR)
  • Right to erasure (Art. 17 GDPR)
  • Right to restriction of processing (Art. 18 GDPR)
  • Right to data portability (Art. 20 GDPR)
  • Right to object (Art. 21 GDPR)

To exercise your rights, contact us using our contact form.

9. Cookies

This site uses Google Analytics (GA4) to understand how visitors use it. GA4 is only loaded, and only sets cookies, after you actively accept the cookie banner shown on your first visit — no analytics request is made to Google before that. You can accept, decline, or change your choice at any time via "Cookie settings" in the footer. Separately, Cloudflare, our content delivery and security provider, may set strictly necessary cookies (for example, to detect and block automated abuse) required to operate the site securely — these apply regardless of your cookie banner choice, since they don't require consent under applicable law. This site also uses Cloudflare Web Analytics for aggregate traffic statistics (e.g. page views, referrers, approximate location). It doesn't use cookies, local storage, or any persistent identifier, and doesn't build a profile of individual visitors, so it runs for all visitors without requiring consent. No other tracking or advertising cookies are used.

10. Data Security

We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your data.

11. Supervisory Authority

You have the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. As a Berlin-based controller, the competent authority is the Berliner Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (Berlin Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information), or any other competent data protection authority.

12. Changes to This Policy

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. Updates will be posted on this page.
